name: CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD UPS Battery Backup
summary: The default pick for any desktop computer with a modern power supply.
verdict: The CP1500PFCLCD has been the go-to UPS for desktop computers for years, and its specifications explain why. CyberPower rates it at 1500VA and 1000W, a higher watt figure than most 1500VA competitors, with a pure sine wave on battery, so it suits the active PFC power supplies in modern gaming PCs and workstations. It is line-interactive with automatic voltage regulation, which corrects brownouts and overvoltage without draining the battery. There are 12 outlets, six on battery and surge and six on surge only, plus a USB data port and CyberPower's PowerPanel software for automatic shutdown. The front LCD shows load, battery capacity and estimated runtime, which makes it easy to check you are within a sensible load. Like every tower UPS, its battery is sealed lead-acid and will need replacing every few years, and runtime at heavy load is measured in minutes.

name: APC Back-UPS Pro BR1500MS2 UPS Battery Backup
summary: The APC equivalent of our top pick, with handy USB charging built in.
verdict: APC's BR1500MS2 is the brand's answer to the CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD, and for a home office it has one useful extra. APC rates it at 1500VA and 900W with sine wave output on battery, which suits computers with active PFC power supplies, and it is line-interactive with automatic voltage regulation. It has 10 outlets, five on battery and surge and five on surge only, and it adds USB-A and USB-C charging ports, so phones and small devices can charge from the battery during an outage without an adapter. An LCD displays load, battery status and estimated runtime, and a USB data port works with APC's PowerChute software for automatic shutdown. The 900W rating is a little below the CyberPower, so it is the better choice for typical home office loads than for the heaviest gaming rigs. As with all tower units, the battery is lead-acid and replaceable.

name: CyberPower CP850PFCLCD UPS Battery Backup
summary: Clean power for office desktops that do not need 1000 watts.
verdict: Not every computer needs a 1500VA UPS. The CP850PFCLCD gives the same pure sine wave output as CyberPower's larger model in a smaller box, rated at 850VA and 510W. That is plenty for a typical office desktop, one or two monitors and a modem and router, which together often draw 150-300 watts. It is line-interactive with automatic voltage regulation, has 10 outlets split between battery-backed and surge-only, and includes an LCD panel and a USB port for CyberPower's shutdown software. The smaller size makes it easier to fit under a desk or in a cabinet, and it usually costs noticeably less than the 1500VA version. The limit is wattage: a gaming PC under load can exceed 510W, and runtime is shorter than the big units, so measure your draw before choosing it over the CP1500PFCLCD.

name: CyberPower CP1500AVRLCD3 UPS Battery Backup
summary: Great value for network gear and electronics, but not for a modern desktop PC.
verdict: The CP1500AVRLCD3 looks almost identical to CyberPower's pure sine model on paper, with 1500VA, 900W, automatic voltage regulation and 12 outlets, six battery-backed. The difference is the waveform: on battery it produces a simulated sine wave, and that is why it costs less. For routers, modems, network switches, TVs, monitors, game consoles and many older computers, simulated sine is fine, and this unit gives a lot of runtime for a low-power load at a good price. Where it falls short is the active PFC power supplies in most modern gaming PCs and workstations, some of which shut off or misbehave on a stepped waveform. If the computer is the main thing you are protecting and it has a recent power supply, spend a little more on the CP1500PFCLCD. If the job is mainly network gear and home theater, this is the better value.

name: APC Back-UPS BE600M1 UPS Battery Backup
summary: The simplest way to keep your internet running through a power outage.
verdict: The BE600M1 is the UPS to buy for internet equipment. APC rates it at 600VA and 330W, which sounds small until you remember that a modem and router together typically draw 15-30 watts, so by manufacturer runtime charts it can keep the internet running for an hour or more. It has seven outlets, five on battery and surge and two on surge only, a USB charging port for a phone, and it can be mounted on a wall near the modem. It is a standby design with a simulated sine wave, which suits network gear perfectly well, and that keeps the price low. It is not the right unit for a desktop computer under load, which can exceed 330W and may not like the waveform. Buy it for the network closet or the shelf where your modem lives, and pair it with a bigger UPS for the computer if you need both.

name: Tripp Lite SMART1500LCDT UPS Battery Backup
summary: A solid office UPS, though the CyberPower and APC picks suit most home buyers better.
verdict: Tripp Lite, now part of Eaton, has long been a staple in small offices, and the SMART1500LCDT is its mainstream desktop model. Tripp Lite rates it at 1500VA and 900W, with a line-interactive design and automatic voltage regulation to correct sags and surges without using the battery. It has an LCD panel showing load and battery status and a USB port for shutdown software. On battery it produces an approximated sine wave rather than a pure sine, which suits networking equipment, monitors and many computers but is not the ideal choice for a modern active PFC power supply. It makes sense where an office already standardizes on Tripp Lite or Eaton gear, or when it is available at a good price. For a home user protecting a gaming or workstation PC, the CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD or APC BR1500MS2 is the cleaner recommendation.
